lesson.title: The Concept That Varies
lesson.summary: Understand the concept that varies from first principles, with a small runnable example.

stage.name: Pattern Principles
stage.subtitle: Book chapters 7–8
stage.description: What patterns are, how to describe them, and the principle of favouring composition over inheritance.

payload.markdown: It’s easy to interpret a design decision once it has been made, but how do you decide where to start? The Gang of Four recommends that you “encapsulate the concept that varies.” In terms of my lesson example, the varying concept is the cost algorithm. Not only is the cost calculation one of two possible strategies in the example, but it is obviously a candidate for expansion: special offers, overseas student rates, introductory discounts, all sorts of possibilities present themselves.

payload.markdown: So how do you spot variation? One sign is the misuse of inheritance. This might include inheritance deployed according to multiple forces at one time (e.g., lecture/ seminar and fixed/timed cost). It might also include subclassing on an algorithm where the algorithm is incidental to the core responsibility of the type. The other sign of variation suitable for encapsulation is, as you have seen, a conditional expression.

items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Composition: Building classes from other objects instead of inheriting from them.
Encapsulation: Bundling state with the methods that touch it, and hiding the rest.
Inheritance: Deriving a class from a base class to reuse and specialise its behaviour.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
